name: THE SCARLET CHEDDAR BURGER (Served with Burgundy Reduction)

recipe.history:
Cheddar cheese traces its origins to the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England, where cheesemakers as far back as the twelfth century discovered that the natural caves of the Cheddar Gorge provided the perfect cool, humid environment for aging wheels of cow's milk cheese. The distinct sharp, tangy flavor of properly aged cheddar develops over months or years as bacterial cultures break down proteins and fats into complex flavor compounds. English cheddar became the dominant cheese of the British Isles and, by extension, of the British colonial world, carried across the Atlantic by settlers who refused to abandon their culinary traditions. The scarlet-orange hue of colored cheddar, achieved today with annatto seed extract, became a regional marker distinguishing certain American cheddars from their paler British cousins, a tradition that began in the 17th century when cheesemakers used carrot juice and marigold petals to signal quality and richness.

When cheddar arrived in the American colonies, it quickly became the country's most consumed and produced cheese, with every farmstead capable of making it from surplus milk. The pairing of cheddar with beef was a natural collision of the two great proteins of Anglo-American agriculture. By the early 20th century, adding a slice of cheddar to a hamburger was already common practice in diners and lunch counters across the Midwest and South. The cheeseburger as a formal menu item is generally attributed to the 1920s and 1930s, with competing claims from California to Oklahoma, but cheddar was always the original choice before processed American cheese began dominating fast-food culture. The Burgundy wine reduction layered into this recipe reaches back to classical French saucery, where the great red wines of the Côte d'Or were reduced with shallots, thyme, and beef stock into glossy, deeply savory sauces that transformed simple proteins into haute cuisine.

I remember the first time I truly understood what sharp cheddar could do to a burger. I was in my early twenties, road-tripping through Vermont in October when the leaves had turned every shade of fire and rust, and I stopped at a farmstand that sold wheels of aged cheddar beside jars of local jam. The woman running the stand sliced me a thick wedge of three-year aged cheddar, and I ate it standing in the cold air beside my car, and the sharpness hit me like a revelation. That evening I stopped at a small pub and ordered a burger, and when they brought it out with a thick slab of local cheddar melted over the patty, I understood for the first time that cheddar on a burger was not a convenience but a commitment. The Burgundy reduction came later, from a winter dinner party where a friend reduced half a bottle of Côte de Nuits into a sauce so gorgeous it made everyone at the table go quiet.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is not a preference — it is an understanding of what beef actually is. When a patty reaches an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the muscle fibers have contracted just enough to firm the exterior while leaving the center yielding, pink, and suffused with its own rendered fat and juice. The Maillard reaction on the exterior crust has created hundreds of new flavor molecules that do not exist in raw or overcooked meat. Beyond 140 degrees, the myosin proteins tighten irreversibly, squeezing moisture out of the patty and into the pan, leaving behind a drier, tougher, less flavorful result. The fat that carries the flavor of the beef — the intramuscular lipids that give a good grind its richness — renders out of an overcooked patty entirely. A medium-rare burger retains all of that. The scarlet interior is not a safety risk when grinding fresh beef from quality sources and handling it properly; it is the correct destination, the proof that you respected both the animal and the craft.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 1/2 lbs freshly ground beef chuck (80/20 fat ratio)
1 bottle (750 ml) Burgundy wine (Pinot Noir, Côte de Nuits preferred)
2 tbsp unsalted butter, cold and cubed
Kosher salt and black pepper to taste
8 oz sharp aged cheddar, sliced thick (1/4-inch slices)
1 red onion, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Combine warm milk and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer; let bloom 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add flour, sugar, and salt to the yeast mixture. Add 3 eggs one at a time, mixing with the dough hook on low speed until a shaggy dough forms.

3. Increase speed to medium and knead 8 minutes until smooth. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time, waiting for each addition to incorporate before adding the next. Knead 6 more minutes until dough is glossy and pulls cleanly from the bowl.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for a slow cold rise.

5. The next day, divide dough into 6 equal portions (about 110g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the dough under itself and pinching the seam. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 3 inches apart.
6. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled and jiggly.
7. Preheat oven to 375°F. Beat remaining egg with 1 tbsp water and brush buns gently. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.
8. Make the Burgundy reduction: Combine wine, shallots, garlic, thyme, rosemary, and bay leaf in a wide saucepan over medium-high heat. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to a steady simmer.
9. Reduce wine by two-thirds, about 25–30 minutes. Add beef stock and continue reducing until the mixture coats the back of a spoon, about 20 more minutes.

10. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing solids. Return liquid to pan over low heat. Whisk in cold butter one cube at a time, then whisk in Dijon mustard. Season with salt and pepper. Keep warm on lowest heat.

11. Make the cheddar béchamel: Melt 1 tbsp butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook 1 minute. Gradually whisk in warm whole milk, bringing to a gentle simmer. Cook 3 minutes until thickened. Remove from heat and stir in grated extra-sharp cheddar, dry mustard, and cayenne until smooth. Season to taste.

12. Form the patties: Gently combine chuck and brisket grinds with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 8 oz each). Form into patties roughly 4.5 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each. Refrigerate 30 minutes.
13. Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.

14. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip once; place 2 thick slices of aged cheddar on each patty. Cook 2–3 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and tent loosely with foil for 3 minutes.
15. While patties rest, halve the brioche buns and toast cut-side down in butter in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

16. Assemble: Spoon a tablespoon of cheddar béchamel on the bottom bun. Place a lettuce leaf, then the patty with melted cheddar. Drizzle generously with warm Burgundy reduction. Add tomato slices and red onion rings. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun.
17. Serve immediately with remaining Burgundy reduction on the side for dipping.
